characters: Adwoa: a fourteen-year-old Ghanaian JHS 2 girl with neat braided hair tied back, wearing a yellow shirt and brown pinafore school uniform, carrying a plain unlabelled notebook.
Kwesi: her thirteen-year-old Ghanaian classmate with short-cropped hair in a yellow uniform shirt and khaki-brown shorts, wearing blue protective nitrile gloves during lab scenes.
Musa: their fourteen-year-old Ghanaian classmate in a yellow uniform shirt and khaki-brown trousers, thoughtful and articulate.
Mr Boateng: the Ghanaian JHS Integrated Science teacher in his late thirties with short neat hair and spectacles, wearing a crisp white lab coat over a blue collared shirt.
Nana Ofori: a respected elderly Ghanaian community elder with grey-flecked hair, draped in rich green-and-gold traditional kente-patterned cloth.

narrationPlan.voice: Thoughtful teen voices for Adwoa, Kwesi, and Musa; crisp, precise teacher voice for Mr Boateng; dignified elder voice for Nana Ofori
narrationPlan.pace: Thoughtful, clear, and investigative (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with distinct, natural voices for each JHS student, teacher, and elder.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason before answering.
Give clear weight to the distinction between suspended mud, living germs, and dissolved heavy metals.

music: Gentle acoustic guitar with flowing river ambience transitioning to a steady, hopeful marimba pulse (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Curriculum Integration: Directly aligns with NaCCA Common Core Programme (CCP) JHS Science (B8.1.1.1: Mixtures and scientific separation methods; Strand 5: Understanding the Environment), Social Studies (B7.1.1.1, B8.1.1.1: Environmental challenges, water pollution, and illegal mining / galamsey), and RME (B8.1.2.1, B9.1.2.1: Caring for God’s creation across Christianity, Islam, and African Traditional Religion).

Scientific Accuracy Guardrail: Emphasises a vital BECE distinction—sedimentation and filtration remove insoluble suspended matter (residue), and boiling kills biological pathogens, but neither removes dissolved toxic heavy metals (such as mercury or lead). Heating mercury-contaminated water in enclosed spaces can also pose vapour hazards, and evaporation concentrates non-volatile dissolved salts and metal ions.

RME & Indigenous Knowledge Respect: Presents Christian stewardship, Islamic Khalifah (trusteeship), and Akan/Ghanaian traditional river buffer taboos side by side as complementary moral frameworks, showing learners the sound ecological reasoning behind indigenous conservation practices.

Adolescent Safety Rule: JHS learners must never visit active mining pits, handle polluted river water without gloves, taste laboratory samples, or confront illegal miners; civic action focuses on supervised buffer-zone tree planting and public education.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated JHS age band and BECE conceptual level?
Is anything here scientifically inaccurate, stereotyped, or unsafe for adolescents?
Verify that the distinction between residue, filtrate, suspended solids, pathogens, and dissolved heavy-metal ions aligns strictly with NaCCA B8.1.1.1.
Check that all three religions in NaCCA RME (Christianity, Islam, and African Traditional Religion) are represented accurately and respectfully.

teacherGuide.overview: An integrated JHS lesson linking chemistry (suspensions, filtration, and dissolved pollutants), civic environmental management (turbidity, water treatment costs, and buffer zones), and comparative religious ethics (stewardship of creation). Designed to prevent persistent misconceptions about water purification before BECE.
learningGoals: Distinguish clearly between a suspension and a solution, and identify residue and filtrate in laboratory filtration.
Explain accurately why filtration and boiling cannot make heavy-metal-polluted water safe to drink.
Analyse the socio-economic impacts of river siltation and illegal mining on downstream communities and water treatment plants.
Compare Christian, Islamic, and African Traditional Religion teachings on environmental stewardship and river conservation.

beforeReading: Show two jars: one with clean tap water mixed with clean garden soil, and one with salt dissolved in clear water. Ask: if we pass both through filter paper, what stays behind and what passes through?
Ask learners what happens to town taps when river turbidity rises too high during heavy rains or upstream mining.
whileReading: Pause after Page 2 and ask learners to define suspension, residue, and filtrate in their own words.
Pause after Page 3 and challenge learners: "Why is Kwesi’s assumption—that clear, boiled filtrate is always safe—dangerous when chemical pollutants are present?"
Pause after Page 5 to connect RME concepts (stewardship, Khalifah, and sacred buffer-zone taboos) to modern Water Resources Commission buffer-zone rules.
afterReading: Safe Lab Practical: Prepare a safe classroom suspension using clean tap water and clean washed sand/clay (never polluted river water). Perform sedimentation, decantation, and filtration, labelling the apparatus, residue, and filtrate.
Draw a three-column comparison table showing what (a) Filtration, (b) Boiling/Chlorination, and (c) Source Protection each prevent or remove.
discussion: Why does preventing heavy-metal pollution at the river source cost society far less than trying to remove dissolved heavy metals at a treatment plant?
How did indigenous riverbank taboos achieve the same ecological outcome as modern Riparian Buffer Zone policies?
reflection: What daily habit in your home, school, or community affects stream and drain cleanliness downstream?

mathsExtension.task: A district water treatment plant normally supplies 12,000 cubic metres of clean water per day. High river turbidity forces engineers to reduce output by 35%. How many cubic metres of water are supplied per day now?
In a laboratory test, 500 mL of muddy water leaves 15 g of dry residue on the filter paper. Calculate the concentration of suspended solids in grams per litre (g/L).

support: Provide a labelled diagram of a funnel, filter paper, residue, conical flask, and filtrate with colour-coded particle icons showing large clay particles trapped and tiny dissolved ions passing through.
stretch: Research how Ghana Water Limited uses coagulation, flocculation (with alum), sedimentation, rapid sand filtration, and chlorination—and explain why raw water above critical Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU) still forces plant shutdowns.

Scientific Accuracy Guardrail: Emphasises a vital BECE distinction—sedimentation and filtration remove insoluble suspended matter (residue), and boiling kills biological pathogens, but neither removes dissolved toxic heavy metals (such as mercury or lead). Heating mercury-contaminated water in enclosed spaces can also pose vapour hazards, and evaporation concentrates non-volatile dissolved salts and metal ions.

RME & Indigenous Knowledge Respect: Presents Christian stewardship, Islamic Khalifah (trusteeship), and Akan/Ghanaian traditional river buffer taboos side by side as complementary moral frameworks, showing learners the sound ecological reasoning behind indigenous conservation practices.

localiseThis: Substitute River Subin with the major river basin serving your district (e.g., Pra, Offin, Birim, Ankobra, Densu, White Volta, or Oti).
Use only clean tap water mixed with clean soil/chalk dust for classroom filtration experiments; never collect water from polluted drains or mining-affected streams.

factCheck.claim: Filtration removes insoluble suspended solids, and boiling kills biological pathogens, but neither removes dissolved heavy metals such as mercury or lead.
factCheck.explanation: Dissolved heavy-metal ions pass straight through filter paper pores and remain non-volatile in water when boiled (with evaporation increasing their concentration in the remaining liquid).
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Common Core Programme (CCP) Integrated Science Curriculum for Basic 7–9 (B8.1.1.1) & WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality.

factCheck.claim: Vegetated riparian buffer zones stabilise riverbanks and reduce sediment and runoff entering streams.
factCheck.explanation: Ghana’s Riparian Buffer Zone Policy (Water Resources Commission) and traditional Ghanaian riverbank taboos both maintain tree/bamboo root networks along stream corridors to prevent bank collapse and siltation.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA CCP Social Studies (B7.1.1.1, B8.1.1.1), RME (B8.1.2.1, B9.1.2.1), & Ghana Water Resources Commission Riparian Buffer Zone Policy.
